en: The Oral Instructions on the Diamond Sutra by the Sixth Patriarch, Zen Master Dajian:

The Dharma-nature is perfectly quiescent; fundamentally, it is without arising or ceasing. Because the thought of arising occurs, there subsequently arises the conditions for birth; thus, Tian-de received his mandate.
By means of this, life arises; therefore, it is called "fate" (*ming*). Once the mandate of Heaven (*tian-ming*) is established, true emptiness (*zheng-kong*) no longer exists as a discrete entity.

The thought-impulses (*nian*) produced on the previous day transform into the mental consciousness (*yi-shi*). The functions of this mental consciousness disperse to become the six sense-faculties (*liu-gen*). Each of these six faculties possesses its own discernment.
That which is the central point of total retention is therefore called the mind (*citta*). The mind is the locus of thought and deliberation;
it is the abode of the spiritual consciousness (*vijñāna*); it is where the true and the false coexist. It is the ground of the critical juncture between ordinary beings and sages.
That all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been unable to escape birth and death is entirely due to this.
Because the mind is burdened by afflictions, the Buddhas teach people only to understand this mind. Once this mind is understood, one sees one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
To see one's own nature is itself *bodhi*. When this [nature] exists as its own essence, it is entirely empty and quiescent, profoundly still.
If there are no conditions, thoughts do not arise; it is only subsequently that they come into being. Where there is arising, there is form. Form consists of earth, water, fire, and wind.
It is a collection of froth, taking blood and qi as its substance, that which living beings rely upon. When the blood and qi are sufficient, the essence (*jing*) becomes sufficient;
when the essence is sufficient, the spirit (*shen*) arises; when the spirit is sufficient, wondrous function (*miaoyong*) arises.
Thus, this wondrous function is precisely the true self at the time of my perfect stillness (*yuanji*); it merely manifests through action because the physical form encounters external objects.

Generally, ordinary beings are deluded and pursue external objects, while sages and worthies are enlightened and respond to them. Those who pursue objects do so from the perspective of "the other," whereas those who respond to objects do so from the perspective of "the self.
To be from the perspective of "the other" is to be attached to what is perceived; thus, one undergoes saṃsāra.

To be from the perspective of "the self" is for the very substance to be eternally empty, remaining as it is through ten thousand kalpas. When viewed in their integration, these are all the wondrous functions of the mind. Therefore, when [it is] as yet...
At the time of birth, that which is called "nature" is perfectly complete, empty and devoid of substance, serene and spontaneous.
Its vastness is equal to space; its coming and going, its transformations, are entirely free.
Even if Heaven were to command me to be born, how could it be possible? If even Heaven cannot command me to be born, how much less so the four great elements? How much less so...

Regarding the five elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*): since there are both the conditions for birth and the causes for birth, Heaven is able to give life to me, the four great elements are able to form my body through their vital energy, and the five elements are able to define me through their numerical categories.
This is why that which has birth must have cessation. Yet, while birth and cessation are one and the same, they differ according to whether one is an ordinary person or a sage.
Ordinary people give rise to thoughts conditioned by existence; consciousness transforms according to karma, and as it is permeated by habitual tendencies, birth becomes ever more intense.

Thus, once born, the mind clings to various delusions: they falsely identify the four elements as their own body, falsely identify their six kin as belonging to them, falsely identify sounds and forms as happiness, and falsely identify worldly toil as wealth.

Noble sir, the perceptions and cognitions of the mind and eyes are without exception false. Once these delusions arise, the afflictions manifest in ten thousand variations. Delusory thoughts usurp the truth, and the true nature consequently becomes obscured.

The notions of self and other become the host, while the true consciousness becomes the guest. The three karmas lead the way in front, followed by a hundred subsequent karmas. One drifts through birth and death without end or limit;
when birth is exhausted, there is extinction, and when extinction is exhausted, one is born again. Such is the nature of arising and ceasing.

In seeking, one falls into the various realms of existence; from one state to another, one remains unaware, further indulging in ignorance and weaving the nets of karma until, after kalpas as numerous as dust motes and sands have passed, one no longer attains a human body.
It is not so for the sages and worthies. The birth of sages and worthies does not depend on thought; they manifest according to their traces.
When they wish to be born, they are born, without awaiting the mandate of that [karmic] life. Therefore, once born, the nature of perfect quiescence (parinirvāṇa) relies upon—
Originally quiescent and without substance, its marks are free from obstruction. Its illumination of the myriad dharmas is like the bright sun in a clear blue sky;

because there is not even a hair’s breadth of concealment or stagnation, it is able to establish all wholesome dharmas throughout the realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, without seeing them as diminished.
It gathers in and sustains all sentient beings, leading them back to nirvana, yet does not regard this as much; they cannot be driven away, nor can they be pursued.
One cannot depart [from this state]. Although one entrusts the four great elements to form a body and the five phases to provide nourishment, these are all merely things borrowed by me;
I have never falsely identified with them as "self. When conditions are exhausted, my traces shall naturally perish. To cast them aside and depart is simply the departure of the Tathāgata;
what has this to do with "me"? Therefore, for ordinary people, where there is birth, there is death. That which perishes cannot but be born again. For the worthy and the sages, however, there is...

Birth also has cessation; that which ceases returns to true emptiness. Therefore, the birth and cessation of ordinary beings are like shadows within the body, entering and exiting in succession without end.
The birth and cessation of sages and worthies are like thunder in the sky, arising and ceasing of its own accord.
One is not burdened by external things. Yet people of the world do not realize that birth and extinction are of such a nature;

instead, they regard birth and extinction as a great affliction and calamity. This is because they lack self-awareness. If one were aware, one would see birth and extinction as mere dust upon the body, which requires only a single shake-off.
How could they possibly burden my nature? In the past, our Tathāgata, out of a heart of great compassion, took pity on all sentient beings.
Thus they are born, deluded, mistaken, and inverted, wandering through birth and death in this manner.
Furthermore, I see that all sentient beings possess an inherently existing nature of bliss and sovereignty, such that all may cultivate and realize Buddhahood.

I desire that all sentient beings exhaustively undergo the arising and ceasing of sages and worthies, rather than the arising and ceasing of ordinary worldlings. Yet, I still harbor concern for all sentient beings who, since beginningless time, have wandered [in saṃsāra].
As time passed, their dispositions had diverged; because they were unable to attain sudden awakening through a single teaching, eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates were expounded for them.
Each gate provides entry, and all lead to the ground of Suchness (*tathatā*).
In expounding each Dharma-gate, he spoke nothing but earnest and truthful words, desiring that all sentient beings, each according to the Dharma-gate they perceived, might enter their own minds.
Upon reaching the ground of one’s own mind-ground, one perceives one’s own Buddha-nature and realizes one’s own Buddhahood; thus, one is identical to the Tathāgata.

For this reason, when the Tathāgata speaks of "existence" in various sutras, he does so desiring to cause all sentient beings to perceive forms and give rise to wholesome states; when he speaks of "non-existence," [he does so for the same purpose].
I wish to cause all sentient beings to leave behind appearances and realize their nature; the teaching that form is empty is likewise intended for this purpose.
Yet sentient beings remain attached, perceiving existence as not truly existent and non-existence as not truly non-existent.

Their views of form and their views of emptiness are both characterized by such attachment, further giving rise to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, which become the very root of birth and death. Thus, I do not point to them the state of non-being.

Second, regarding the Dharma-gate: furthermore, because their delusions, errors, and inversions cause them to drift through birth and death even more intensely than before, the Tathāgata further preached the Great Prajñāpāramitā Dharma for them.

This serves to shatter the two views of permanence and annihilation, enabling all sentient beings to know that true existence and true non-existence, as well as true form and true emptiness, are fundamentally non-dual. They are not distant from people; they are profoundly still and tranquil, existing right here.
Within one's own nature, by using the wisdom of that very nature to illuminate and shatter all delusions, one sees clearly for oneself.
Therefore, the six hundred fascicles of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* are all the Tathāgata’s teachings on Buddha-nature for bodhisattvas who have attained the fruit.
Nevertheless, among these [teachings], there are still those spoken for the sake of the sudden and the gradual;

only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is spoken for the sake of those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna, and for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle. Therefore, that sūtra first speaks of the four modes of birth and the four marks, and subsequently states:
"Whatever has marks is all empty and false. If one perceives all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. This is intended to reveal—
All dharmas reach the state of non-abiding; this is the ultimate truth.

Therefore, in this sutra, whenever the Tathāgata speaks of anything pertaining to existence, he immediately negates it, so as not to directly grasp at the true mark (lakṣaṇa) for the sake of showing it to sentient beings.

This is because he fears that if sentient beings do not understand what the Buddha has taught, their minds will instead become attached to something. As it is said: "The Buddha-dharma is itself not Buddha-dharma."
This is of that category.
*The Oral Instructions on the Diamond Sūtra* (end).
*The Essential Compendium of Commentaries and Treatises on the Diamond Sūtra*, two fascicles.
*Jingang jing shu lun zuan yao kan ding ji* (A Compendium of the Essential Points of the Commentary and Treatise on the Diamond Sutra), compiled by Zongmi of the Tang dynasty;
recorded by Zixuan of the Song dynasty. In four fascicles.
